facts.claim: Training with mixed precision and the Adam optimiser takes 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for 16-bit weights, 2 for 16-bit gradients and 12 for the optimiser’s 32-bit copy of the weights, momentum and variance (Rajbhandari et al., 2020, the ZeRO paper).

ZeRO shares out the optimiser state across the data-parallel copies (stage 1, 4× less memory), then the gradients too (stage 2, 8×), then the weights (stage 3, less with every copy added); stages 1 and 2 send no more than plain data parallel, stage 3 sends 1.5× as much (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).
By the ZeRO paper’s count, GPT-2 with 1.5 billion parameters needs at least 24 GB to train with mixed-precision Adam, though its 16-bit weights alone take 3 GB (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).

A transformer layer’s saved activations take s·b·h·(34 + 5·a·s/h) bytes for s tokens, b sequences, hidden size h and a heads; with the layer split t ways and the attention scores recomputed, 34·s·b·h/t (Korthikanti et al., 2022).
GPipe splits a model into K stages on K chips and each batch into M micro-batches; the idle time, the bubble, is O((K−1)/(M+K−1)), and it was negligible when M ≥ 4×K (Huang et al., 2019).
Megatron-LM splits each transformer layer across chips with only two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass (Shoeybi et al., 2019).

Splitting inside a layer should generally go up to the number of GPUs in one server, with pipeline stages across servers; the authors trained a 1-trillion-parameter model at 502 petaFLOP/s on 3,072 GPUs this way (Narayanan et al., 2021).
NVIDIA lists the H100 SXM with 80 GB of memory (NVIDIA’s H100 page, checked October 2026).
NVIDIA lists the H100 SXM at 1,979 teraFLOPS of BF16 with sparsity, twice its dense rate (NVIDIA’s H100 page, checked October 2026).
Inside a DGX H100 box, eight H100 GPUs talk over NVLink at 900 GB/s per GPU (NVIDIA’s DGX H100 user guide, checked October 2026).

Between boxes, each GPU in a DGX H100 has its own ConnectX-7 port at up to 400 Gb/s, or 50 GB/s (NVIDIA’s DGX H100 user guide, checked October 2026); Llama 3’s clusters also used 400 Gbps links between GPUs.
Meta’s Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, a model dimension of 8,192 and 64 attention heads (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Llama 3 405B began pre-training with batches of 4M tokens in sequences of 4,096 tokens (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Meta reports using 38–43% of the GPUs’ BF16 peak while training Llama 3 405B on 8,192 to 16,384 H100s (Llama 3 paper, 2024).

Over a 54-day stretch of Llama 3 405B’s pre-training on up to 16,384 H100s, Meta counted 466 job interruptions, 419 of them unexpected, GPU issues the largest share (58.7%), and still kept over 90% of the time training (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Young (1974) gave the best time between checkpoints as about √(2δM), for δ the time to write one and M the mean time between failures.
Daly (2006) refined Young’s interval with a higher-order estimate that also counts the time to restart.
